utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise a preliminary matter. Mr. Groome, before you do so, could I ask you whether it's of such urgency that we have to deal with it right away or that it could wait until after we have heard the evidence of Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does relate to the evidence of Mr. Theunens, and it does relate to the redirect examination that we will conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. And I thank you again for adjourning the redirect of Mr. Theunens. It has given us an opportunity to consider the cross-examination and its implications for how we proceed. Mr. Weber has prepared his redirect examination and will address the specific challenges made to Mr. Theunens's evidence during the cross-examination. I want to begin my submission by tendering the report. There could be no need to rehearse the extensive discussions and guidance regarding the first part of the report. I have carefully considered the guidance and all of the relevant factors and have prepared a second redacted version of the report. This is somewhat different from the first redacted report that we had proposed. Over the last two days, we have once again carefully reviewed the first part of the report. We have redacted additional material, material which Mr. Weber amply covered in direct examination. We have unredacted some material related to General Kadijevic's role and authority and the Vance Plan, two topics dealt with in some detail on cross-examination. So at this time the Prosecution tenders or would ask the Chamber to replace the current report that's now been given the exhibit number P3029 MFI with a new redacted version of that report, the 65 ter number is 28612a. I would inform the Chamber that there was a technical problem this morning in uploading the English version of that report. That should be resolved in the next hour and a half, but I would ask the Chamber to rule on that at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't have an issue with the Prosecution replacing one redacted version with another. That's, I think, within their prerogative. I do still maintain an objection as to the admissibility of this report as an expert report. I think the cross-examination has raised serious issues as to whether this gentleman is an expert, including the criteria that their own former chief military analyst specified for experts being the same rank or higher with similar command experience as the target accused. I propose, therefore, that the MFI status remain and that the Chamber consider the evidence given and yet to be given before making a determination as to whether the report can be accepted into evidence as an expert report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, apart from the former chief military analyst which said that experts should be of the same rank or higher with similar command experience, is there any legal authority to support that position, I mean the Chamber, so that we can orient ourselves on any case law on the matter or any --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- specific legal writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On that particular matter, there is none. As to whether a military analyst can be considered an expert witness, there is case law. From the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic, the decision as to Philip Coo, disqualifying him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that has been raised several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Raised, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking specifically for that aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Groome, of course the -- it's uploaded now. The 65 ter number you mentioned may replace the version of the expert report, especially part 1 as it was uploaded until now and as it was MFI'd, I think. But of course, the Chamber will need some further time to consider admission also now after having heard Mr. Ivetic's objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have a relative --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is still a bit more to my submission. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I'll -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The second part of the my submission relates to the evidence cited in the report. The Mladic Defence has made a general challenge to the methodology of the report, Mr. Theunens's use of an analytical methodology referred to as the intelligence cycle. He has made this challenge through his questions and by tendering into evidence a scholarly article from Professor Hulnick that questions the reliability of the intelligence cycle as a methodology and suggests that it is likely to result in a mischaracterisation and misunderstanding of the underlying source material. The Defence case, as I understand it, is that the Chamber must not rely on or must place little weight on the contents of the report and what it says about the evidence cited in the report. I have spent the last two days giving careful consideration to this, the guidance, the Chamber's often expressed preference for the Prosecution to tender a minimum number of documents to establish its case. The Chamber has instructed us to review the bar table motion related to military documents and provide notice about which document -- documents we still intend on tendering and to do that seven days from today. We will do that, but I want to be frank with the Chamber in that we will still be tendering a substantial amount of this evidence, documentary evidence directly related to the acts and conduct of Mr. Mladic, documents which go to core elements of his responsibility. We will do so for the following reasons. The issue now squarely before the Chamber is whether Mr. Theunens's expert report, which relied solely on the intelligence cycle for its analysis of evidence, is reliable. The only way for the Chamber to adjudicate this issue is to review the evidence which Mr. Theunens drew his conclusions from. The Chamber itself, during the examination of Mr. Theunens, expressed the importance of and its intention to look at the underlying documents when assessing Mr. Theunens's evidence. This occurred in the context of Mr. Ivetic's objection at transcript page 20344, that it would be improper for the Chamber to rely on the evidence of Theunens alone with respect to background factual issues. The Chamber responded to Mr. Ivetic by stating: "In the evaluation of evidence, of course, the Chamber will not just rely on what the witness says but also the documentary, on the documents underlying what the witness expressed as his expert opinion." This expression of the Chamber's approach with respect to the determination of background factual matters makes it all the more imperative for the Prosecution to adduce the underlying documentary evidence which directly establishes the criminal liability of General Mladic. The orders he signed, the reports he received. The Prosecution considers that this expression by the Chamber correctly reflects the Prosecution's position as well as the ample jurisprudence on this matter. As set out in some detail in our 31st of October, 2013, submission, Mr. Theunens's expert report facilitates the Chamber's understanding of the evidence. It is not intended as a substitute for it, nor is it a legal alternative to evidence required in making essential findings of criminal liability in this case. It is also difficult for me to imagine a judgement that in significant part cites as a basis for a factual finding the report of Mr. Theunens and what he said about unadmitted evidence, a judgement without reference to the source evidence itself because it was never tendered by the Prosecution. It is difficult for me to imagine that the Appeals Chamber would place its imprimatur on a judgement that took this approach. And I can't imagine the Appeals Chamber would excuse my failure to discharge my statutory duty to tender evidence sufficient to establish Mr. Mladic's responsibility. So again we will carefully review the documents in that bar table and again file the notice as instructed, but it is likely it will still be a substantial number of documents. I accept that the Chamber may decline to admit some or all of this evidence. I simply ask that it be done on the basis of legal principles and criteria applicable to the admission of evidence and that undue focus not be placed on the number of documents. Finally, Your Honours, the Chamber asked us to consider redactions to P3011, marked for identification. That exhibit is entitled: "The Law on the Army," and dated 1 July 1992. It is the actual law governing the Army of the Republika Srpska and sets out the essential command relationships and operational mechanisms of the army. It is signed into law by Radovan Karadzic and is perhaps one of the most important documents in the Prosecution's case. It is cited by each of the military experts and even other experts as well. In fact, it is cited by Mr. Theunens over 35 times in his report. The Prosecution maintains its position that the entire document should be admitted into evidence. I appreciate that it is 54-and-a-half pages long, but given its central importance I believe it requires its admission into evidence in total unredacted. Thank you, Your Honours. And Ms. Stewart informs me that 28621a is now properly uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. I'd like to make already the following short observation. When you refer to what the Chamber expressed on page 20344, that, of course, was in the context of what was challenged at that moment by Mr. Ivetic, that was about defence plans, specific identified portions of the report. But we'll further consider the matter. Apart from that, you also made some observations about -- let me just have a look. Well, we'll have a look at what documents you still deem fit to be tendered. Of course, the Chamber will, as given as its guidance earlier, that to the extent the evidence is challenged, and you referred especially to the methodology and the challenge to the -- the cycle being a wrong approach, the intelligence cycle to be a wrong approach, leading to misinterpretation of the underlying evidence. Of course, the Chamber will also consider to what extent this general theoretical position has been substantiated in relation to specific parts of the report; that is, to explain to the Chamber why this methodological flaw, as presented by the Defence, would have its -- had its effect on the conclusions drawn by this witness. I leave it to that at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, although the Chamber understood Mr. Groome primarily -- since you objected to the admission of the newly redacted report, since -- although Mr. Groome, in the view of the Chamber, mainly announced what he's going to do and why he's going to do that, which is usually not a matter on which I would seek a response by the Defence, but if nevertheless if you would like to bring anything to our attention in this context, please don't hesitate to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I agree with your analysis. I don't think a response is required to what Mr. Groome has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Then, I'm looking at the clock now already. Reason is that I have a -- an agenda on procedural matters which will, it's my estimate that it will take anything between 40 and 50 minutes to deal with entirely. I don't want to do it now because Mr. Theunens asked to be released as quickly as possible. I just raise it for the parties that if they would need so much time for the re-examination and perhaps then again further examination by the Defence, that we would not have that 40 to 45 or 50 minutes left, that it would inevitably result in at least to have a hearing tomorrow. I just inform the parties about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I assist the Chamber for scheduling purposes. Mr. Weber anticipates that his redirect examination will take approximately 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then there is a fair chance that depending on what the Defence will then claim as time still needed, there is a fair chance that we would deal with all the procedural matters today as well. Let's move forward and ask Mr. Theunens to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Theunens. I again remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration given at the beginning of your testimony, and I also would like to inform that everyone in this courtroom expects your testimony to be concluded today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber will now reexamine you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On Tuesday, at transcript pages 20561 to 63, the Defence asked you about your reference to General Kadijevic's published memoir. During this examination, the Defence challenged that your conclusions were based on what it claimed to be your sole reliance on this document as a single source of your opinions. At page 20563, you indicated that you did not rely on this single source but you also had contemporaneous documents, including General Kadijevic's orders and guidelines. First, do I understand correctly that General Kadijevic's published memoir is one of many sources that you reference in relation to your analysis of the transformation of the JNA between 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As part of this analysis, I'd like to ask you more specifically, do you also reference General Kadijevic's contemporaneous directives and orders?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I think it's also good then to put all the material or all the references you have mentioned now in context with the specific military documents, including those of the 9th JNA Corps covering the -- the relevant time-period; i.e., the latter half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In reaching your conclusions on the transformation of JNA, do you also rely upon orders from Blagoje Adzic, the published daily notes of Borislav Jovic, and the decisions from the SFRY Presidency in addition to the materials you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And when it concerns, because you also talk about transformation in 1992 or the first month of 1992, I refer to the documents issued by the 2nd Military District and its subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you also analyse as part of this section materials related to General Mladic, including his closing speech and tasks for the commanders of the 9th JNA Corps on 15 January 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours. And this is footnote -- I mean, there is an excerpt in footnote 420 in part 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the challenge by the Defence, the Prosecution in accordance with the Chamber's guidelines now tenders the related materials. The additional materials being tendered relate to the transformation of the JNA. The ones from General Kadijevic are 65 ter 08303a, 17330, 03845, 17332, and 14349. The additional materials from Blagoje Adzic, Borislav Jovic, and the SFRY Presidency being tendered are 65 ter numbers 08267, 08568a, 07239, 14389, and 17333. In addition to this, we tender General Mladic's 15 January 1992 9th Corps closing speech and tasks, which is uploaded under 65 ter 17334. We're tendering all these as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You refer to 11 exhibits. We would invite Madam Registrar, first of all, to reserve 11 numbers now, and then to prepare a short list in which these numbers appear. The numbers to be reserved, Madam Registrar, will be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Numbers P3078 up to and including P3088, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These numbers are reserved and Madam Registrar will prepare a list. Mr. Ivetic, any objections to these source materials on which the witness relies in relation to the, if I could say so, the Kadijevic part of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Defence takes no position since it's in relation to the guidelines of Your Honour. We take no position and make no additional objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then once the numbers are assigned, these 11 exhibits are admitted into evidence. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On Tuesday, at pages 20564 to 20581, the Defence examined you about the Vance Plan and whether or not actions were taken to circumvent it. During this examination, you were shown a document from General Mladic which appears to date sometime in early January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the record, this document is now Exhibit D451.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At transcript page 20575, the Defence claimed that this document, which includes details of the Vance Plan, gives "a better picture of where General Mladic stood in relation to the Vance Plan and its success." Before we discuss some additional materials, do you recall your related testimony in this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did this January 1992 document show that General Mladic had specific knowledge and awareness of the terms of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At page 20579, the Defence attempted to have you confirm that this document, in fact, shows that General Mladic seemed to support the Vance Plan rather than trying to subvert it. You responded that one has to be careful in drawing conclusions from one document, and then you referred us to additional materials from General Mladic at footnote 585 of part 1 of your report. Before discussing the additional examples that you've referred us to, could you please tell us when UNPROFOR was deployed to monitor the implementation of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the resolution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, if I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I'm still trying to find exactly on page 2579 that one has to be careful in drawing conclusions from one document. Let me -- 579. Yes. Yes, but I'm still looking at that page, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would direct the Chamber's attention to lines 17 to 19 on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Yes. Thank you. Please proceed. Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the deployment of UNPROFOR followed the adoption of two Security Council resolutions which can be -- I mean, this can be found on page 177 of part 1 of the report. First, we have seven -- sorry, Security Council Resolution 743, 21st of February, 1992, and then we have 749 on the 7th of April, 1992. In practice, the deployment of UNPROFOR was gradual; i.e., not all forces arrived at the same time in the different UNPAs and became operational at the same time. I -- if I -- my recollection is well -- is correct, I believe, for example, in Sector East in April/May UNPROFOR became fully operational, and this has to be April/May 1992. But in others sectors, for example, Sector South, my recollection is that it took more time before UNPROFOR became fully operational. And if you allow me, I did not have the opportunity to make an additional comment during cross-examination on the document, the early January 1992 document by General Mladic, which I think may be useful to further clarify the context of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Please go ahead --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- Mr. Theunens, if you feel it's important for us to be aware of.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was that at that time that the political leader of the Krajina Serbs, Milan Babic, rejected the Vance Plan; whereas the president of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic, had agreed to the plan and wanted to use all available means to convince the Krajina Serbs of accepting the plan. My view is that General Mladic's document where he explains the benefits of the Vance Plan and the importance of strict adherence is part of the plan or the campaign by Mr. Milosevic to convince the Krajina Serbs of accepting the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 14421, page 4 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Appearing before you is a 27 February 1992 report and order from General Mladic sent to the 2nd Military District IKM in Manjaca. At the end of this document, General Mladic communicates he has decided to continue to assist the TO and MUP of the RSK in carrying out organisational and establishment changes and in equipping the TO and MUP units. There is also reference to his decision to clean up the town of Drnis and its environs. Can you tell us whether or not this document is consistent or not with your conclusions that the JNA 9th Corps took actions to circumvent the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- yes, Your Honours, it is. And this document is also cited in footnote 585 on page 179 of part 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 14421 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the underlining in the part you read is not part of the original and should be ignored by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is. It's just how we received it, so it's nothing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You received it, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that it has no specific meaning, but I'm just wondering what it is. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14421 receives number P3089, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 00769, page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, appearing before you is a 5 April 1992 report from General Mladic to the 2nd Military District. At the end of this report, General Mladic indicates again that he decided to continue with the mobilisation, forming, equipping, and arming in this case of mobilised units in Bosansko Grahovo and Bosanski Petrovac and to continue helping the RSK TO and MUP in forming TO and MUP units in the 9th Corps zone of responsibility. Again, could you tell us whether or not this document is consistent with your conclusion that the JNA 9th Corps took actions to circumvent the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours. I mean, it is. I would just like to clarify, I mean, Bosansko Grahovo and Bosanski Petrovac are located in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's a different subject. It is not RSK MUP and TO as is explained in the next paragraph in the document, and this is also a document I have cited in footnote 585, mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 769 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00769 receives number P3090, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. Let me just have a look. Do I understand your testimony well that it's only the lines where it says "to continue helping the RSK TO Main Staff and the Ministry of the Interior in forming of TO and MUP units," that that's the only part which is demonstrative for circumventing the Vance Plan, whereas the first part is not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, that is -- that was the purpose of my comment on the first part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's okay with you, I'm happy at this stage or I can continue going through five more documents and asking the same exact question. If it's okay with you, I could tender these collectively for the same exact purpose that I have been asking on the previous two documents. So if acceptable, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 763, which is a -- another report from General Mladic, along with additional reports from General Mladic under 65 ter 741, 752, and 775. In addition to this, we tender 65 ter 753, which is General Mladic's plan relating to the regrouping of RSK TO and MUP units between the months of February and March 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my information, Mr. Weber, these are all footnote materials to the relevant part? Of course, I couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they are, then the Chamber would, starting from the view that it's -- that the witness considers these materials relevant for the conclusions drawn. If not, I think they should be put to the witness first and the question to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Two are and I can put the other three, if that's what Your Honour would like to do. I'd be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or another option would be to give the texts of these exhibits to the witness during the break and ask him, upon return, whether he found in those documents elements which are in support of his conclusions. There are two ways. But I think since we have time, the best way to do it would be to put the three to the witness now. The two other ones who are in footnote materials, could you already identify those so that we decide on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: 65 ter 763 and 65 ter 753.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, any objection against them being admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter 763 receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P3091, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 65 ter 753.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P3092, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Weber, with the other three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 741.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, coming up before you will be a 3 March 1992 request to carry out mobilisation from General Mladic, sent to the 2nd Military District command. If you could please review the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have read the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Just so you see the complete document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have the second page of the English translation. It's just the signature page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have any comments in relation to this document and your opinions on the JNA 9th Corps's activities after the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- could we go back to the first page for the content of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- now knowing who signed it? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I would also like to see the third paragraph because the third paragraph, actually -- in the first two paragraphs talk about preparations in Bosnia-Herzegovina where General Mladic requests his superior -- excuse me. Where General Mladic proposes mobilisation of -- of a number of TO units in Bosansko Grahovo and Bosanski Petrovac for potential engagement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the third paragraph is actually a clarification of that. So, I mean, this document is not related to any -- any support or, yeah, activities in -- concerning the RSK MUP or TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that might have been my -- that's obviously my bad in my reading of the document. If I could check the other two, then, to see if that repeats during the recess. However, based on Mr. Theunens's explanation, I believe that Mr. Mladic's involvement of mobilisation of units in Bosnia would separately make this document relevant and we ask that it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It may make it relevant for something else if evidence were to be led, but if it is not part of Mr. Theunens's analysis and it does not go toward points raised in cross, I don't believe redirect is the proper time to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, any direct link to the evidence of this witness? Apart from that it's not related to what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I apologise for the confusion. We could separately bar table this. I -- I appreciate, based on my mistake, that I -- I misunderstood the -- the context of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The witness has clearly explained it, and Mr. Ivetic did bring up the general activities of the accused during this time-period. In the specific contents -- context in relation to the Vance Plan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I think you are using a lot of words where most important is that you made a mistake in considering this to be relevant as underlying material for Mr. Theunens. If we leave it to that and if you would not tender this document at this time in this way, then we could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry, I mean -- I'm not answering a question now, but it provides information on the preparations taken by the 9th Corps to mobilise certain TO units. This is -- this looks like regular units of the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it's in specific municipalities. And if you see that in the context of what I have described on the changing role of the JNA and also the role of the 2nd Military Districts, it could be part of that. But what I tried to explain in my answer to the question was it has no relation with the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On Tuesday, at transcript pages 20608 to 11, the Defence and the Chamber questioned you about why you did not include a declassified CIA intelligence report dated 28 May 1995 in your report. Based on the information that is in this CIA report and on the CIA web site, it appears that this document was declassified on 19 March 2013. Can you just clarify for the record whether or not this CIA report was even available to you when you completed your report in September 2012?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I also -- I received an e-mail from a former colleague, I think, one or two months ago, where the declassification of these documents, I don't know, hundreds of -- apparently, hundreds of documents by the CIA -- actually, declassification is by another authority, but that these documents would become available on the CIA web site. And this is like, I think, two or three months ago. But I never had time to -- to look at the web site. And obviously, this is long after this report was finalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you were asked to by the Chamber to review these approximately 300 documents that were recently declassified, would be willing to do so and let us know whether or not this would change or impact any of your opinions?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's always useful to look into additional material. I mean, it would be, I think -- in my specific case, it would mainly depend on my supervisor, whether I would be authorised to spend time on doing this, but I would find it, I mean, very interesting to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the -- what you had access to during the preparation of your report. Did you have unfettered access to the evidence collection in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate number of documents that are available in this collection? I mean, I'm speaking of the overall evidence collection of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- my -- I would make a guess just based on the documents I have seen over the years I worked here, but I would say more than hundred thousand, several hundred thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During the drafting of your report in this case, was there any direction or indication provided to you from the OTP trial team that affected your analysis or any of your conclusions from your review of the documentary material?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During cross-examination, the Defence asked you generally about whether you ever assisted the Prosecution either by drafting, reviewing, or revising briefs. You specified your limited role and you also distinguished in your answers between your involvement before April 2009 and thereafter. Can you clarify whether or not you have participated in the drafting of anything other than your report for the OTP in this case? So aside from your report in the Mladic case.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe already -- I already mentioned that. But for this case, i.e., the Mladic case, I only compiled -- I only prepared this report here. I did not provide any other work or support or assistance to the Office of the Prosecutor or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just at this point to take care of a quick housekeeping matter. The Prosecution did locate the most recent curriculum vitae of the witness from the Hadzic case and we have uploaded and provided the 65 ter to the Defence. It's uploaded under 65 ter 30523 and we tender it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30523 receives number P3093, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this is a good time for the break. This would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is a good time for the break. There is, however, one matter which you caused to be in the air now. If the Chamber would ask Mr. Theunens, which the Chamber did not do, to review any CIA documents which now have become -- they have been declassified. Of course, the Chamber didn't do that, so therefore whatever the witness said about it, whether he would be willing, whether his chiefs would be willing to give him that time is irrelevant at this moment. At the same time, Mr. Ivetic, you referred to one of those CIA documents which seems to indicate that you are aware of these documents, these documents having been declassified. And if those documents would contradict or undermine the opinions of this witness, of course the Chamber would expect you to put them to the witness and to confront him with that material while he is here before us. Therefore, I'm putting the two together. The Defence has shown to be aware of those documents, has not put specific elements to the witness any further than it did. And you have considered whether this witness, if he would be asked, what he's not, to further consider whether that material would change any of his conclusions -- well, it is not put by the Defence to him that it would change his conclusions. So in the absence of any further action, the Chamber will just leave the matter as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of evidentiary -- what we intend to rely on, we intend to rely on Mr. Theunens's analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: However, in visiting the web site, I do see that there is many materials that may be consistent that were not put to Mr. Theunens. So I don't want to get into a full-on process and I understand the Chamber's concern, but if this is a significant issue to the Defence where they feel it impacts his methodology, we would ask for the opportunity to tender additional materials from this web site to show that there is materials consistent with his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at this moment on the basis of what the Defence has put to the witness, you do not consider this to be a concrete challenge of the conclusions of Mr. Theunens, and for that reason you refrain from now tendering and further seeking to be admitted into evidence any of those reports where -- which the Defence is apparently aware of, and you're asking that whether -- if at any later point in time the Defence would raise such challenges, that you would still have an opportunity to further rely on those materials, perhaps when cross-examining any witness the Defence may present, if it ever comes to a Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think the procedural context of these matters is now clearly put on the record. We take a break and we'll -- after Mr. Theunens has left the courtroom, we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Could the usher escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Weber, you would consider the last two out of the five documents which you considered to tender in support of the undermining of the Vance Plan. Have you made up your mind in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I have, and on further review I think they might be relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- to the other thing that the witness indicated and not necessarily what [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you, but I strike them from the list of five supporting documents. So two now remain, which are footnote materials already and which have been admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On Tuesday, at pages 20581 to 92, the Defence asked you about Arkan. During this examination, you were read a portion of your testimony from the Karadzic case related to Arkan's presence in Bosnia in late September 1995. In particular, this was in relation to a 23 September 1995 document from General Mladic. You were also read parts of General Mladic's order related to paramilitaries from July 1992. Do you recall this testimony?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 09685.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you is an order from Tomo Kovac dated 11 October 1995. What does this document show with respect to the relationship between the VRS, the RS MUP, and Arkan?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document shows co-operation between the VRS, i.e., VRS Main Staff, and the MUP at the -- I mean, the MUP at the level of the minister because it refers to an agreement. And then at -- when we're looking at the contents of the order, it indicates that Arkan will be used or his group will be used to arrest -- to start arresting deserters from the front in the territory of the Prijedor CJB, organise, I mean, military ranks; i.e., bring them back into the military and return them to their original brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, we saw during cross-examination that General Mladic's order from 28 July 1992 indicated that paramilitary formations were to be disarmed and arrested if they did not place themselves under the unified command of the VRS. Also, according to the text of General Mladic's 23 September 1995 document, he also appears not to be satisfied because Arkan did not report to any command from the battalion level to the VRS Main Staff to receive an assignment. In light of this subsequent order, what does this show about the Main Staff's attitude towards paramilitary groups, like Arkan's SDG, who were operating in the zones of responsibility of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, reading this order the -- the 11th of October document, it is not exactly clear under whose orders Arkan operates, but at least, I mean, his presence is tolerated by the VRS Main Staff, and he's also given explicit missions. Whereas, when we go back to the -- the earlier order, the one from July 1992 which is mentioned, for example, in footnote 292 and 293, there paramilitaries who, quote unquote, are honourable -- whose intentions are truly honourable, quote/unquote, and place themselves in the service of the just struggle for the survival of the Serbian people, i.e., as is explained further on, incorporate themselves in the units of the VRS, these units again can remain and will then form a part of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if you look at the English translation, in the first line: "Pursuant to the agreement between the MUP Minister and the Chief of the VRS General Staff Manojlo Milanovic." I think this is a mistake in the English translation. In the original, it's clear it refers to Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for noting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should carefully review that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With that being noted, if it's okay to rely on original in relation to the individual identified which is clearly Manojlo Milovanovic. The Prosecution at this time tenders 65 ter 09685 into evidence. The Prosecution also tenders 65 ter 06764, which is the 23 September 1995 document from General Mladic which was referred to during the Defence cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter 0965 receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, was it 09685?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 685. Yes, which then receives?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P3094, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Then 65 ter 06764.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P3095, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, P094 and P095 certainly are not the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The numbers are P3094 and P3095 [Realtime transcript read in error "P0394 and P0395"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3094 and P3095, and that's the numbers that were assigned in the last line by Madam Registrar to these two documents, are admitted into evidence. It seems that at line 11, the 0s and the 3s have changed place. The numbers I mentioned are the numbers under which they are now [Realtime transcript read in error "not"] in evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30553.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, during cross-examination you were asked questions about the co-ordination, resubordination, and what you also referred to as the attachment of MUP units during VRS operations. In particular, on page 20615, the Defence, in leading into this examination, made passing reference to your testimony related to Trnovo. Before you is a 23 July 1995 SRK regular combat report from Dragomir Milosevic at the IKM in Trnovo. This document is sent to the Main Staff. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours. I don't believe that I included it in my report for the Mladic case, but I have certainly included it in my report for the Stanisic-Simatovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Weber. I have, unfortunately, to deal with the transcript. Page 29, line 15 and 16, now reads that: "The numbers I mentioned are the numbers under which these documents are not in evidence." But what I think I said is that the numbers I mentioned, P3094 and P3095, are the numbers under which they are now in evidence. Please proceed and sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What does this document or report show in terms of the relationship between the SRK and the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at least on the first page in -- under title 2, it shows that the Skorpions unit is considered a unit of, quote/unquote, our forces, which in my view indicates that it's subordinated to the SRK during the conduct of operations that are discussed in this combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 30553 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30553 receives number P3096, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Approximately three questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. Which means anything between two or four, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at the document we have on the screen, sir, and if we can ask you to look at the first paragraph, it would appear that the 4th DLpbr and the MUP, Ministry of Interior, Skorpions are forces that are in the same area but not necessarily at the same point. You will agree with me, sir, from the military standpoint when it talks about the point of convergence between the MUP, Ministry of Interior, Skorpions and the 4th DLpbr, Drina Light Infantry Brigade, seems to imply that they are operating in separate zones, does it not? Rather than being comingled forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yeah. I mean, each unit has its own areas of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree from a military standpoint that one has to take into account neighbouring force even if they are not subordinated but are still friendly forces to prevent so-called blue on blue contact?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I mean, we spoke about co-ordination with neighbouring forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So this document could also be in relation to co-ordination and reporting on neighbouring forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, you have to look at the originator from the document. The document originates from the Sarajevo -- from the SRK, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the VRS. They have a number of forces. I mean, they have what I would call establishment units, i.e., units that are always part of the SRK, as well as other units, for example, the MUP Serb -- as it is identified, MUP Serbia units Skorpions, who are operating in the zone of operations of the SRK in the Trnovo area. And looking at the document, and again the other documents in the context of the operations that are conducted in Trnovo, I conclude that this MUP unit is subordinated to the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can call up what has now been marked as P3094.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you are referring to P3094.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it's correct on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is the order of the MUP minister in relation to Arkan. I'd like to ask you, sir, if the MUP is using Arkan in October 1995, despite General Mladic's September 1995 appeal to President Karadzic and to the MUP to withdraw and remove Arkan, can we thus conclude that Arkan and his group fall under the jurisdiction of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, before answering the question I think we have to be careful in how we phrase this, because you -- you use the word "despite," but I see the document that there is agreement between the MUP -- I mean, MUP RS at minister level and the Main Staff through its chief or the deputy commander of the VRS General Manojlo Milovanovic. It is not -- I mean, maybe there is -- sorry, on -- at -- looking at this document only, I cannot draw a conclusion as to whom Arkan is subordinated at that time. Maybe there is a military document that also describes the role of Arkan, because I would assume that for the VRS, the commanders in the area, they would also like to know, and through their chain there has to be a communication of the agreement that's been reached. And then looking at these documents in combination, we would be in a better position to draw a conclusion as to who Arkan is subordinated while conducting these specific type of activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, could I ask you one question in this context. Arresting deserters. Deserters of what armed force in your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my understanding, Your Honours, this includes for sure members of the VRS. Because maybe you remember what I mentioned earlier, that I had a recollection that Arkan had been sent to arrest deserters. People in general were afraid of Arkan, and not just non-Serbs but also among the Serbs. And again, I don't think I specifically saw this document before but this is something I remember from my work on -- on the Balkans, that Arkan could be used for those kind of activities; i.e., that he would be sent to the rear area. And just the fact that he and his people were there would have an intimidating role --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you're now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- going beyond my question. My question was: Deserter of what armed force? And then you explained why it would be useful to use him for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I therefore understand that the -- that there is an agreement in which the chief of VRS GS is involved, which includes Arkan to be used in the arrest of deserters of the VRS and to bring them back to their original brigades. Is that how we have to understand this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, to bring them back to their original VRS brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is the role and the function of Arkan and his men. I take it it's not Arkan alone. Under whose command he did so you say not clear from this document. So the function, the role is clear, but under whose command, if any, he performed that task is unknown. Is that a correct understanding of your interpretation of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The -- the 23rd of September letter from General Mladic to Mr. Karadzic suggests that the presence at that stage, i.e., end of September 1995, has not been approved by the VRS Main Staff; i.e., that Arkan is not operating under the orders of the VRS Main Staff in September 1995 in the -- the wider Sanski Most area. Now we are, I would say, three weeks later, and then we see that there is an agreement between the Main Staff and the MUP on the use of Arkan. But I cannot conclude from this 11 October document under whose authority Arkan is doing -- is conducting the activities that had been -- have been agreed between the MUP and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at least you conclude from this document that it is with the consent of the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And not, I mean, "consent," but in the military sense explicit approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it just as likely a reading of this document that there was an agreement reached that military forces in an area and police forces in an area will arrest personnel with each providing the units from their composition which would participate in such a task such that the inclusion of Arkan may not even have been known to the army Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't understand the question, because Arkan is explicitly mentioned there. And if, I mean, from a practical sense, if Arkan or members of his group are conducting certain activities in an area, it will be known. And people will ask questions, what are they doing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if you look at the addressee, the Republika Srpska General Staff, "for their information," isn't it entirely possible that this document could be the first time that the Main Staff is getting information that indeed Arkan is the group that will be doing the previously agreed to arresting?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand why you -- I mean, previously there is an agreement and then the agreement has to be communicated to everybody so that everybody is familiar with what has been agreed to. And that when they see Arkan or other units identified in this order, when they see them conducting certain activities, that nobody is surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to see where apparently the possible disagreement lies. The order reads "pursuant to the agreement," and then mentions the two parties, that is, the MUP and the chief of the VRS Main Staff. Then orders who should start arresting people. Is it true that there are two ways of reading this document? The one is that the agreement already included who would do these arrests or that the agreement was more limited, dealing with people having to be arrested but without giving the details on who would do that. And that in this order, it is further specified who would perform those arrests. Is that, Mr. Ivetic, the two ways of interpreting the document, whereas it's your position that the second interpretation I mentioned is the -- the better one and that the first one apparently is what you understood to be the interpretation given by Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now we have at least clarified or identified what the problem is. Mr. Theunens, could you please comment on the preferred understanding of the document by the Defence. To which I add, Mr. Ivetic, there seems to be no disagreement that even if the original agreement would not identified who would have to do the arrests, that at least through this order the Main Staff becomes aware, if not already before, who would be assigned with this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, please, your comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I still -- I mean, I am trying to practically imagine how this agreement would be implemented. And while doing so, I find it hard to understand that the -- I mean, if I understand the second interpretation well, that there could be an agreement to arrest VRS members, and then on the ground, people would discover that, yeah, by the way, also Arkan is involved. I mean, it wouldn't make sense --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I intervene, then, for a second. utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will deal with quite a number of procedural matters. I'll start with the Prosecution's request to admit into evidence a stipulation between the parties. I think it was a matter mainly dealt with by Mr. McCloskey. On Tuesday, the Chamber denied the Prosecution's 4th of December, 2013, motion to admit into evidence a stipulation between the parties, which had been filed on the record on the 19th of November, 2013. This filing of the 19th of November was made on behalf of both parties and clearly set out what was stipulated to. On Tuesday, the Prosecution raised an issue about the legal status of such stipulations. The Chamber has previously taken the view that agreed facts should be made part of the record by stipulating in court or filing them on the record. I refer to transcript page 101 as an example. And the parties have filed numerous agreements on certain facts. Agreed facts or stipulations which have been put on the record are materials on which the parties can rely on future submissions. An agreement on matters of fact removes these facts from the area of dispute between the parties and will make it highly unlikely that any of them will present evidence to the contrary of what was agreed upon. Similarly, reasons for not accepting the agreed facts for the truth of their content are unlikely to be found by the Chamber when making its final findings. However, the Chamber is not bound by any point of fact or law agreed upon between the parties and recorded in a filing under Rule 65 ter (H) of the Rules. The ultimate weight of these agreed facts will be determined by the totality of the evidence. Whether or not a separate decision on admission is taken, the status of the agreed facts which are recorded is not any less than evidence formerly tendered and admitted under Rule 89(C) of the Rules. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that formal admission of the agreed facts would constitute an unnecessary procedural step. And under these circumstances, the Chamber's denial of the Prosecution's 4th of December, 2013, motion stands. I move to the second item, unless the Prosecution would raise any issue in relation to this first one.
