utterances.text: Madam Registrar, once the complete document, including the cover page, has been uploaded, it may -- it may replace the existing version of P2900. I move now to deliver the decision -- the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's motion to add Mile Micic to its witness list and to admit his evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. On the 11th of November, 2013, the Prosecution filed a motion to add Mile Micic to its Rule 65 ter witness list and to admit his evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. In doing so, the Prosecution argues, inter alia, that the inclusion of Micic on its Rule 65 ter witness list is in the interests of justice, given that his evidence is both relevant and probative. Further, the Prosecution states that whilst it previously did not present this witness to avoid presenting every available witness account on all issues, it now finds it appropriate to request the witness's addition. This is because, according to the Prosecution, Micic's prior testimony clearly establishes the date that Tolimir instructed Witness Milenko Todorovic to prepare Batkovic camp to receive prisoners from Srebrenica. With regard to the Prosecution's request to admit Micic's evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, the Prosecution tenders seven pages of his prior testimony from the Prosecutor versus Tolimir trial, dated the 4th of July, 2011. The Prosecution submits that this evidence is relevant to Counts 2 to 8 of the indictment. Further, the Prosecution highlights that Micic's evidence does not concern the acts and conduct of the accused and is corroborated by Witness Ljubomir Mitrovic's Rule 92 bis evidence, Witness Novica Simic's Rule 92 quater evidence, and Todorovic's Rule 92 ter evidence. The Defence did not respond to the Prosecution's motion. The Chamber will first consider the addition of Micic to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list. At the outset, the Chamber recalls and refers to the applicable law concerning amendments to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list as set out in its previous decision filed on the 22nd of August, 2013. The Chamber considers that the witness's evidence is prima facie relevant and of probative value. The Chamber considers that whilst the Prosecution has not shown good cause to add the witness to its Rule 65 ter witness list at this stage, the addition of the witness will result in a limited additional burden for the Defence, in particular given that the witness's evidence relates to issues that have been addressed by other witnesses. In this respect, the Chamber notes that the Defence has not responded to the motion. The Chamber has also considered that the Prosecution proposes to tender the witness's evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, and that the evidence consists of seven pages of transcript of the witness's prior testimony in the Tolimir trial. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber finds that it is in the interests of justice to allow the addition of Mile Micic to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list. The Chamber will now consider whether to admit Micic's evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Chamber recalls and refers to the applicable law concerning admission pursuant to Rule 92 bis, as set out in its previous decision filed on the 19th of October, 2012. Having reviewed the proffered excerpts of Micic's prior testimony, the Chamber notes that the witness provides evidence on General Tolimir's movements on the 12th of July, 1995, and considers that the testimony relates to an important aspect of the case; namely, the charges in the indictment related to Srebrenica. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the proffered evidence is relevant, as required under Rule 89(C) of the Rules. The Chamber further notes that the proffered evidence does not concern the acts and conduct of the accused and is of a cumulative nature to the evidence of Ljubomir Mitrovic, Novica Simic, and Milenko Todorovic. The Chamber considers that there are not other factors under Rule 92 bis(A)(ii) weighing against admitting the tendered evidence in written form. Accordingly, the Chamber grants the motion and admits into evidence the excerpts of Mile Micic's prior testimony from the Tolimir trial as specified in Annex E of the Prosecution's motion. The Chamber instructs the Prosecution to upload the above document into e-court and requests the Registry to assign this document an exhibit number. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Could I ask whether the excerpt has already been uploaded into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll -- perhaps, Madam Registrar, if you would already reserve a number for the excerpt of the transcript of the testimony of Mr. Micic in the other case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The reserve number would be P3097, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision on admission stands. It's just a matter of technicality to have the accurate 65 ter number uploaded into e-court, which will then be the underlying document, P -- and again I see on the transcript we have a 03 instead of a 30 to start with. P3097. I move to my next item. It relates to the uploading of new witness packages related to the 27th 92 bis decision and concerns Witness RM074 and Witness Sakib Muhic. By informal communications of the 27th of November and the 6th of December, the Prosecution requested permission to upload new attestation and statement packages, replacing those attestations currently uploaded for RM061 and RM074. The Chamber hereby allows the Prosecution to upload those new packages but will revisit the matter after it has reviewed them. I move to my next item which is a reminder, a reminder about further submissions from the parties on revisions made in the text of intercepts tendered with Milan Babic. Mr. Groome, I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, last Tuesday you asked us to address you orally today and I'm prepared to do that if that's convenient now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it -- because it's not only -- let me just put on the record the context. It was indeed on the 10th of December, last Tuesday, that the Chamber requested the Prosecution to give some clarification on the revisions made in the texts of intercepts tendered with Milan Babic. The Prosecution was invited to address the reliability of the documents in light of the suggested revisions, and the Defence was also invited to set out their position on this matter. And it is at this point, Mr. Groome, that I would give you an opportunity to first make any submissions on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Chamber asked us to address two issues: First, who made the suggested revisions; and b, to address the reliability of the documents. The Chamber raised this inquiry and referred to 15 specific intercepts. We note that one of those, 65 ter 20351, does not in fact have revisions. First, Your Honours, I think it's important to recognise what is not at issue here, and nothing about these revisions raises issues related to the authenticity of the audiotapes. This issue is confined to the reliability of the transcripts of those audiotapes and the translation of those transcripts. As to the first part of the Chamber's inquiry, the revisions were made prior to this case and they were made by language assistants in the Office of the Prosecutor. The process involved required those language assistants to listen to the audiotapes and to recheck the B/C/S transcripts, and then check the corresponding translations. As to the second part of the Chamber's inquiry, with respect to reliability, the Prosecution's position is that the suggested revisions address minor adjustments and do not put into question the reliability of these intercept transcriptions. These minor adjustments are consistent with the evidence the Chamber has already heard with respect to the accuracy of these transcripts by Witness RM507, who talked about the omission of some words and the background voices that can sometimes be heard on intercepts. The Prosecution -- I'll now go through some of the -- or all of the individual intercepts that the Chamber has drawn our attention to. On review of the 15 intercepts, the Prosecution notes that the revisions generally fall into the following categories: First, background conversation unrelated to the conversation between the main speakers. For example, in 65 ter 20112, there is an unidentified female voice talking in the background which has now been added to the transcript, in the revised transcript. The Prosecution does not rely on anything that this person says in the background. The second category: Foreign language terms and names. For example, 65 ter 20507, the word "Salzber" [phoen] other "Salzburg" [phoen] has been replaced with "Strasbour" [phoen] or "Strasbourg," though it's very clear from the context of the conversation they are talking about the European Parliament, which is based in Strasbourg. There are typographical errors that occurred when transcribing the audio. For example, in 65 ter 20405, we see in the English at e-court page 7 that the phrase "other things as well" has been seemingly corrected even though text in the English remains the same. "Other things as well." That's because the correction in the transcript is of the B/C/S "idrugo" to "i drugo," introducing a space between the words in e-court page 5. There are a number of revisions in many of these transcripts which are of this nature. I shouldn't say "many," in a number of these transcripts. For example, 65 ter 20441, "odma," although correctly translated as "immediately," has been changed to "odmah," [phoen] adding an h. This was simply a typo, understood as such, by those who translated the document into English. There are also grammatical errors that occurred in the B/C/S when transcribing the audio. For example, 65 ter 20298, we can see in the English at e-court page 12, the phrase "in Stari Grad," has been seemingly corrected even though the text in the English remains the same, "in Stari Grad." That's because the B/C/S at e-court page 13 uses the phrase "u Stara Gradu" has a declension error that has been corrected in the original transcription. Your Honour, I can address the remainder of these if the Chamber wishes. I think the Prosecution -- I think the point that we're trying to make is that these revisions have no significant evidential import on the substance of the transcript, and we believe that they are inconsequential. Of course, now both the Chamber and the Defence have these suggested revisions, and if at any time the Defence in looking at the revisions thinks that it is of substance, the Prosecution would certainly work with them to come to an agreement about what the correct revision should be. And certainly the Chamber could make its own decision about whether anything was of consequence. But we have reviewed them and we do not believe that any of the revisions change in any way the substantive import of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. I would not be surprised if the Defence could not immediately respond to this. But having looked at the material itself, is there anything the Defence would like to raise either on the basis of their own review of the material or on the basis of what Mr. Groome just told the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could perhaps just be clearer, when I extended that offer to work with the Defence to correct anything that they believe is substantive, I did not intend to mean today but over the course of the coming months or the course of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe Tuesday it had been said that we could also respond in writing by Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it would be the more efficient manner for us to see -- to take a look at those in front of us today and respond in writing, although I don't think there will be anything substantial from our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then -- you're right, we gave an opportunity either to make submissions orally today or in writing by tomorrow. Since you have looked at the materials yourself and having now heard the observations made by Mr. Groome, may I take it that it would still be feasible to submit such comments in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for the Defence to make the further written submissions on the matter. I move on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we leave that. It seems that I've misspoken. At line 21, I intended to say 20 -- 65 ter 20411. Page 62, line 21, should be "65 ter 20411." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That must be on another page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't see not even a number what comes close to it on page 61, line 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it's page 62, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The correction is clear now, that you referred to 65 ter 20411 and not to 20441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the transcript was already corrected on page 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move on. And I'm moving now to the Prosecution request for order on pseudonyms. On the 27th of November, the Prosecution made an oral request that the Chamber issue an order with regard to the pseudonyms of protected 92 bis and quater witnesses. The Chamber take this opportunity to put on the record that for those witnesses who have been granted protective measures, including the use of a pseudonym, the case-specific RM reference numbers assigned are the official pseudonyms. Most of these can be found in the Prosecution's 10th of February, 2012, witness list. I move to my next subject which deals with exhibits tendered with Witness Barry Hogan. On the 27th of November, the Prosecution was asked to provide the Chamber with additional information with regard to Exhibit D381 and its relation, if any, to videos bearing 65 ter numbers 22311F and 1D1310. The Chamber is still awaiting this information. On the same day, the Chamber admitted the video excerpt marked as D385 but understands from the Registry that we are still awaiting the 65 ter number to be provided by the Defence as well as the video on disk. The Chamber hereby sets the dead-line of the end of business tomorrow for the parties to provide the information needed and for the Defence to provide D385 on disk. The next item on my agenda deals with scheduling. The Chamber previously discussed the further scheduling with the parties. As matters stand now, the Chamber expects to hear the oral Rule 92 bis submissions in the last week of February. A Scheduling Order will follow, but the parties should already prepare according to this indication. I move to the next item, assuming that there is nothing the parties want to raise in relation to scheduling issues at this moment in addition to -- to what we have dealt with already. I would like to consult for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there anything apart from this scheduling issue the Chamber just addressed a minute ago in relation to the 98 bis submissions that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we should go to private session for one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you know, we asked for six months. We were allocated five months. We accept that. But I hope that Your Honours would still reconsider that if the Prosecution reopens their case in March. And in the line with our request, that if the reopening would last for two weeks, that we would need at least one month to extend the time of the beginning of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Decisions are usually taken on the basis of what is said in Latin to be rebus sic stantibus, which means as matters stand at that moment. We have been put on notice that the exhumations may trigger a request for reopening the case by the Prosecution. We'll consider that, and, of course, at that point in time consider what the consequences would have to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And for 98 bis, we would comply with Your Honours' order, so we will be ready to have oral arguments at the end of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you will deliver those oral arguments, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask your permission to maybe empower my colleague Ivetic to be here alone at that time, since both me and Mr. Stojanovic will be in the field, I'm sure, at that time. And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, any specific -- because the ruling until now was that Mr. -- that there were two members of the Defence team which would be allowed to cross-examine witnesses and make submissions but only related to those witnesses they were cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, so now we are making the application for Mr. Ivetic to be here alone and address you on 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oral motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution -- takes the Prosecution any position in Mr. Ivetic delivering -- not only delivering the 98 bis submissions but also being there without counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no objection to Mr. Ivetic. Certainly, he could give the entire submission while Mr. Lukic is in the room. The one concern that I would have is that it's -- what's become clear over the course of this trial, is that Mr. Mladic seems to rely, in significant part, on the counsel who is not addressing the Chamber. And I think the more prudent course of action would be, once the Chamber has issued its scheduling order, Mr. Lukic and Mr. Stojanovic could consider whether they could be here; and if not, then maybe they could raise it again at that stage. But it seems to me to be a bit premature to not give Mr. Mladic the benefit of both of his counsel, as it seems that it's been something that's been important to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't like this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't like the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was very polite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's straight-forward. Yes, now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it stresses your importance, the answer of Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, but at the wrong time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, importance is not limited in time, Mr. Lukic. It's for eternity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will revisit the matter in due course. And whether that would mean that we either grant your request or that we'll wait until a further stage and a renewed request be made and then decide upon it, I leave that entirely open at this very moment. But we will consider it and we'll inform the parties. The Chamber expects that the preparations for the 98 bis submissions, which are of a kind -- at least I take it you'll not do it by heart in court. That needs to be written out anyhow. That you can continue at this moment to prepare, to the extent you can prepare at all, before the final evidentiary stage has been concluded. So we'll revisit the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's what -- all we had, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we are -- I have only one and a half item left. I think, as a matter of fact, no item at all -- no, we have two items left which will take so little time that I suggest that we'll proceed and then adjourn for the day. The first is documents MFI'd with Mr. Theunens. Before today's hearing, we had three leftovers; that was P3029, which we have to leave MFI'd anyhow because a new redacted version will appear, and we had P3054 and P3075. Any further submissions on P3054 MFI'd until now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Nothing further from the Defence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing further from the Defence. Prosecution also.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And P3075?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Likewise nothing further on that one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Same for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If my recollection and the recollection of my staff serves me and us well, P3054, I think we needed the extraction of the letter from a newspaper article without the remaining text. Has that been done until now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait to decide on that until we have heard from the Prosecution that it has been done. For P3075, it was a missing B/C/S version, I think, which has been uploaded meanwhile and that for that reason there is no objection against admission. P3075 is admitted into evidence. Finally, the last item is about P3011, which was admitted into evidence with Witness Treanor. The Chamber has admitted P3011 into evidence on the 2nd of December of this year, and it then requested the Prosecution to review the document in order to identify which exact portions the Prosecution would like to have in evidence. You have made those submissions now, Mr. Groome. What then remains is the position of the Defence in relation to this matter. That is the full document still needed to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It may assist my colleagues to know it's the Law on the Army dated the 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where you said you would need -- you have reviewed it but you are still of the opinion that you would need all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Defence has no objection on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was to some extent the Chamber's concern whether it was not too much, although pages alone are not determining the thoughts of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Being comforted that the Prosecution has, as always, seriously considered the issue raised by the Chamber, and in view of the fact that the Defence does not object, P3011 is -- was already admitted but remains admitted as the full text of that law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you're still on your feet or again on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour said you had two additional matters. Is the Chamber finished? I just have one thing that I think I need to say. It may be clear to everyone but it should be on the record. Mr. Theunens was the last witness we intended to call. We appreciate that the Chamber is still considering some of our 92 bis and quater motions as well as the bar table motions. Once we have had a chance to review these decisions and determine that there remains nothing else for the Prosecution to do with respect to its case in chief, I will file a written notice that we have rested our case, and I expect that we would be able to do this shortly after the Chamber's last decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any comments from the Defence? I would say it almost goes without saying that not knowing the Chamber's decision on many outstanding motions, that it would be a bit difficult for the Prosecution to already do anything else than to provisionally say that -- that you have presented your evidence, but depending on what is still to wait for, that that might change and that you will give written notice of your position once we have decided on all the evidentiary issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn for the day and we adjourn sine die, and since -- you never know what happens, but since I do not expect to see you again before the Christmas, whether we are talking about the 25th of December or whether we are talking about the Orthodox Christmas, I wish everyone, parties, you, Mr. Mladic, my colleagues, everyone assisting us in and just outside this courtroom, the Chamber conveys its best wishes, best greetings for these days, and hope to see you back somewhere in January all in good health. We adjourn sine die.
